div.head: MEMB. 2. SUBSECT. 1.
Causes of Heroical love, Temperature, full Diet, Idleness, Place, Climate, &c.
div.p:
Of all causes the remotest are stars. Comment. in convivium Platonis.Ficinus cap. 19 saith they are most prone to this burning lust, that have Venus in Leo in their Horoscope, when the Moon and Venus be mutually aspected, or such as be of Venus’ complexion. Lib. de audiend. Poet.Plutarch interprets Astrologically that tale of Mars and Venus, in whose genitures ♂ and
♀ are in conjunction, they are commonly lascivious, and if women, queans; as the good wife of Bath confessed in Chaucer;

But of all those Astrological Aphorisms which I have ever read, that of Cardan is most memorable, for which howsoever he be bitterly censured by Comment. in Genes. cap. 3.Marinus Mersennus, a malapert Friar, and some others (which Et si in hoc parum a praeclara infamia stultitiaque abero, vincet tamen amor veritatis [And if in this I’m hardly free from flagrant infamy and stupidity, yet the love of truth will prevail].he himself suspected), yet methinks it is free, downright, plain and ingenuous. In his Edit. Basil. 1553. Cum Commentar. in Ptolemei quartipartitum.eighth Geniture or example, he hath these words of himself. ☌♀♄ & ☿♄ in ☿ dignitatibus, assiduam mihi Venereorum cogitationem praestabunt, ita ut nunquam quiescam. Et paulo post, Cogitatio Venereorum me torquet perpetuo, & quam facto implere non licuit, aut fecisse potentem puduit, cogitatione assidua mentitus sum voluptatem. Et alibi, ob ☾ & ☿ dominium & ♄ radiorum mixtionem, profundum fuit ingenium, sed lascivum, egoque turpi libidini deditus & obscaenus [The conjunction of Venus, Saturn and Mercury, with Saturn in the dignities of Mercury, will be responsible for my incessant thinking about sex, so that I’m never calm. And shortly afterwards: The thought of sex constantly tortures me, and the passion I couldn’t satisfy by action, or I was ashamed to have acted on when I was able, I’ve feigned by constant thought. And elsewhere: On account of the eminence of the Moon and Mercury, and the intermingling of the rays of Saturn, I had a profound but lascivious genius, and I was indecent and addicted to filthy lust]. So far Cardan of himself, quod de se fatetur ideo Fol. 445, Basil. Editionis.ut utilitatem adferat studiosis hujusce disciplinae [which he confesses about himself in order to provide a service to students of this discipline], and for this he is traduced by Mersennus, when as in effect he saith no more than what Gregory Nazianzen of old, to Chilo his scholar, offerebant se mihi visendae mulieres, quarum praecellenti elegantia & decore spectabili tentabatur meae integritas pudicitiae. Et quidem flagitium vitavi fornicationis, at munditiae virginalis florem arcana cordis cogitatione foedavi [eye-catching women were offering themselves to me, and the integrity of my chastity was tested by their exceptional elegance and striking beauty. And in truth I have escaped the disgrace of fornication, but defiled the flower of virginal purity with the secret thoughts of my heart]. Sed ad rem [But to the point]. Aptiores ad masculinam venerem sunt quorum genesi Venus est in signo masculino, & in Saturni finibus aut oppositione, &c. Ptolemaeus in quadripart. plura de his & specialia habet Aphorismata, longo proculdubio usu confirmata, & ab experientia multa perfecta, inquit commentator ejus Cardanus. Tho. Campanella Astrologiae lib. 4 cap. 8 articulis 4 & 5, insaniam amatoriam remonstrantia, multa prae caeteris accumulat aphorismata, quae qui volet, consulat. Chiromantici ex cingulo Veneris plerumque conjecturam faciunt, & monte Veneris,
de quorum decretis, Taisnerum, Johan. de Indagine, Goclenium, ceterosque si lubet, inspicias [Those with Venus in a masculine sign in their geniture, and in the house of Saturn or opposed to it, etc., are more disposed to lust after men. Ptolemy in the Four Books has more about these things, and particular aphorisms, undoubtedly confirmed by extensive practice and perfected by much experience, as his commentator Cardan says. Tommaso Campanella, Astrology Bk 4, ch. 8 articles 4 and 5, amasses many aphorisms, more than the others, denouncing erotic madness, which anyone who wants to can consult. Palm-readers conjecture very many things from the Girdle of Venus, and the Mount of Venus, on whose doctrines, if you want, you can look at Taisnier, Johannes de Indagine, Goclenius and the rest]. Physicians divine wholly from the temperature and complexion; phlegmatic persons are seldom taken, according to Ficinus Comment. cap. 9, naturally melancholy less than they, but once taken they are never freed; though many are of opinion flatuous or hypochondriacal melancholy are most subject of all others to this infirmity. Valescus assigns their strong imagination for a cause, Bodin abundance of wind, Gordonius of seed, and spirits, or atomi in the seed, which cause their violent and furious passions. Sanguine thence are soon caught, young folks most apt to love, and by their good wills, saith Dial. amorum.Lucian, would have a bout with everyone they see: the colt’s evil is common to all complexions. Theomestus a young and lusty gallant acknowledgeth (in the said Author) all this to be verified in him, I am so amorously given, you may sooner number the Sea sands, and snow falling from the skies, than my several loves. Cupid hath shot all his arrows at me, I am deluded with various desires, one love succeeds another, and that so soon, that before one is ended, I begin with a second; she that is last is still fairest, and she that is present pleaseth me most: as an Hydra’s head my loves increase, no Iolaus can help me. Mine eyes are so moist a refuge and sanctuary of love, that they draw all beauties to them, and are never satisfied. I am in a doubt what fury of Venus this should be: alas, how have I offended her so to vex me, what Hippolytus am I! What Telchine is my Genius? Or is it a natural imperfection, an hereditary passion? Another in Num. 32.Anacreon confesseth that he had twenty sweethearts in Athens at once, fifteen at Corinth, as many at Thebes, at Lesbos, and at Rhodes, twice as many in Ionia, thrice in Caria, twenty thousand in all: or in a word, εἰ φύλλα πάντα [if {you can count} all the leaves], &c.

lg.l: Canst count the leaves in May,
Then count my loves I pray.

div.p: His eyes are like a balance, apt to propend each way, and to be weighed down with every wench’s looks, his heart a weathercock, his affection tinder, or Napthe itself, which every fair object, sweet smile, or mistress’ favour sets on fire. Guainerius tract. 15 cap. 14 refers all this to the hot temperature of the testicles, Ferrandus a Frenchman in his Erotique Mel. (which Printed at Paris 1624, seven years after my first Edition.book came first to my hands after the third Edition) to certain atomi in the seed, such as are very spermatic and full of seed. I find the same in Aristot. sect. 4 prob. 17, si non secernatur semen, cessare tentigines non possunt [if the semen is not emitted, the lustful desires cannot stop], as Guastavinius his Commentator translates it, for which cause these young men, that be strong set, of able bodies, are so subject to it. Hercules de Saxonia, hath the same words in effect. But most part I say, such are aptest to love that are young and lusty, live at ease, stall-fed, free from cares, like cattle in a rank pasture, idle and solitary persons, they must needs hirquitallire [become like a goat], as Guastavinius recites out of Censorinus.

l.hi: Mens erit apta capi tum quum laetissima rerum,

lg.l: Ut seges in pingui luxuriabit humo.
The mind is apt to lust, and hot or cold,
As corn luxuriates in a better mould.

div.p:
The place itself makes much wherein we live, the clime, air, and discipline if they concur. In our Mysia, saith Galen, near to Pergamum, thou shalt scarce find an adulterer, but many at Rome, by reason of the delights of the seat. It was that plenty of all things, which made Gerbelius descrip. Graeciae.Corinth so infamous of old, and the opportunity of the place to entertain those foreign comers; every day strangers came in, at each gate, from all quarters. In that one Temple of Venus a thousand whores did prostitute themselves, as Strabo writes, besides Lais and the rest of better note: all nations resorted thither, as to a school of Venus. Your hot and Southern countries are prone to lust, and far more incontinent, than those that live in the North, as Bodin discourseth at large, Method. hist. cap. 5, molles Asiatici [soft Asiatics], so are Turks, Greeks, Spaniards, Italians, even all that latitude: and in those Tracts, such as are more fruitful, plentiful, and delicious, as Valencia in Spain, Capua in Italy, domicilium luxus [the dwelling of debauchery] Tully terms it (which Hannibal’s soldiers can witness), and Canopus in Egypt, Sybaris, Phaeacia, Baiae, Tota Cypri insula delitiis incumbit, & ob id tantum luxuriae dedita ut sit olim Veneri sacrata [The whole island of Cyprus devotes itself to pleasure, and is therefore so dedicated to wantonness that it was once consecrated to Venus]. Ortelius. Lampsacus olim Priapo sacer ob vinum generosum, & loci delitias [Lampsacus, in former times dedicated to Priapus because of its excellent wine and the pleasures of the place]. Idem.Cyprus, Lampsacus. In Leander Albertus in Campania.Naples the fruits of the soil and pleasant air enervate their bodies, and alter constitutions: insomuch, that Florus calls it Certamen Bacchi & Veneris [a battleground
between Bacchus and Venus], but Lib. de laud. urb. Neap.Foliot admires it. In Italy and Spain, they have their stews in every great City, as in Rome, Venice, Florence, where as some say, dwell ninety thousand Inhabitants, of which ten thousand are Courtesans; and yet for all this, every Gentleman almost hath a peculiar Mistress; fornications, adulteries are nowhere so common: urbs est jam tota lupanar [the whole city is now a brothel]; how should a man live honest among so many provocations? Now if vigour of youth, greatness, liberty I mean, and that impunity of sin which grandees take unto themselves in this kind shall meet, what a gap must it needs open to all manner of vice, with what fury will it rage? For, as Disputat. de morbis animi, Rainoldo Interpret.Maximus Tyrius the Platonist observes, libido consequuta quum fuerit materiam improbam, & praeruptam licentiam, & effrenatam audaciam, &c. [when lust has pursued a base object, and rash licentiousness, and unbridled audacity, etc.], what will not lust effect in such persons? For commonly Princes and great men make no scruple at all of such matters, but with that whore in Spartian, quicquid libet licet, they think they may do what they list, profess it publicly, and rather brag with Proculus (that writ to a friend of his in Rome, Lampridius. Quod decem noctibus centum virgines fecisset mulieres [That in ten nights he had turned a hundred virgins into women].what famous exploits he had done in that kind) than anyway be abashed at it. Vita ejus.Nicholas Sanders relates of Henry the 8th (I know not how truly) quod paucas vidit pulchriores quas non concupierit, & paucissimas non concupierit quas non violarit, he saw very few fair maids that he did not desire, and desired fewer whom he did not enjoy: nothing so familiar amongst them, ’tis most of their business: Sardanapalus, Messalina, and Joan of Naples, are not comparable to If they contain themselves many times ’tis not virtutis amore, non deest voluntas sed facultas [from love of virtue: it’s not the will that’s lacking but the power].meaner men and women; Solomon of old had a thousand Concubines, Ahasuerus his Eunuchs, and keepers, Nero his Tigillinus, Panders and Bawds, the Turks, Muscovites, Moguls, Shereefs of Barbary, and Persian Sophies, are no whit inferior to them in our times. Delectus fit omnium puellarum toto regno forma praestantiorum (saith In Muscovia.Jovius) pro imperatore; & quas ille linquit, nobiles habent [A selection of all the outstandingly beautiful girls in the whole kingdom is made … for the Tsar; and those he leaves behind, the nobles take]; they press and muster up wenches as we do soldiers, and have their choice of the rarest beauties their countries can afford, and yet all this cannot keep them from adultery, incest, sodomy, buggery, and such prodigious lusts. We may conclude, that if they be young, fortunate, rich, high-fed, and idle withal, it is almost impossible they should live honest, not rage, and precipitate themselves into those inconveniencies of burning lust.

lg.l: [Idleness ruined both the kings and prosperous cities

div.p: Idleness overthrows all, Vacuo pectore regnat amor, love tyrannizeth in an idle person. Amore abundas Antipho [You’re overflowing with love, Antipho]. If thou hast nothing to do,

thou shalt be haled in pieces with envy, lust, some passion or other. Homines nihil agendo male agere discunt [Men learn to do evil by doing nothing]; ’tis Aristotle’s Simile, Polit. 8 num. 28.as a match or touchwood takes fire, so doth an idle person love.

Quaeritur Aegistus quare sit factus adulter, &c., why was Aegisthus a whoremaster? You need not ask a reason of it. Ismenodora stole Bacchon, a woman forced a man, as Pausanias Atticis lib. 1. Cephalus egregiae formae juvenis ab aurora raptus quod ejus amore capta esset [Cephalus, a youth of singular beauty, was carried away by Aurora because she was captivated by love for him].Aurora did Cephalus: no marvel, saith In amatorio.Plutarch, Luxurians opibus more hominum mulier agit: she was rich, fortunate and jolly, and doth but as men do in that case, as Jupiter did by Europa, Neptune by Amymone. The Poets therefore did well to feign all Shepherds Lovers, to give themselves to songs and dalliances, because they lived such idle lives. For love as E Stobaeo ser. 62.Theophrastus defines it, is otiosi animi affectus, an affection of an idle mind, or as Amor otiosae cura est sollicitudinis [Love is the concern of the idler].Seneca describes it, Juventa gignitur, luxu nutritur, feriis alitur, otioque inter laeta fortunae bona; youth begets it, riot maintains it, idleness nourisheth it [and leisure amid the delights of good fortune], &c., which makes Principes plerumque ob licentiam & adfluentiam divitiarum istam passionem solent incurrere [And most princes usually rush into this passion because of licentiousness and abundance of riches].Gordonius the Physician cap. 20 part. 2 call this disease the proper passion of Nobility. Now if a weak judgement and a strong apprehension do concur, how, saith Hercules de Saxonia, shall they resist? Savonarola appropriates it almost to Monks, Friars, and religious persons, because they live solitary, fare daintily, and do nothing: and well he may, for how should they otherwise choose?

Diet alone is able to cause it: a rare thing to see a young man or a woman that lives idly, and fares well, of what condition soever, not to be in love. Plutarch. vit. ejus.Alcibiades was still dallying with wanton young women, immoderate in his expenses, effeminate in his apparel, ever in love, but why? He was over-delicate in his diet, too frequent and excessive in banquets. Ubicunque securitas, ibi libido dominatur; lust and security domineer together, as St. Jerome averreth. All which the wife of Bath in Chaucer freely justifies.

l.hi: For all to sicker, as cold engendreth hail,
A liquorish tongue must have a liquorish tail.

div.p:
Especially if they shall further it by choice Diet, as many times those Sybarites and Phaeaces do, feed liberally, and by their good will, eat nothing else but lascivious
meats. Vina parant animos veneri.Vinum imprimis generosum legumen, fabas, radices omnium generum bene conditas, & largo pipere aspersas, carduos hortulanos, lactucas, Sed nihil erucae faciunt, bulbique salaces. Improba nec prosit jam satureia tibi. Ovid.erucas, rapas, porros, caepas, nucem piceam, amygdalas dulces, electuaria, syrupos, succos, cochleas, conchas, pisces optime praeparatos, aviculas, testiculos animalium, ova, condimenta diversorum generum, molles lectos, pulvinaria, &c. Et quicquid fere medici impotentia rei venereae laboranti praescribunt, hoc quasi diasatyrion habent in delitiis, & his dapes multo delicatiores; mulsum, exquisitas & exoticas fruges, aromata, placentas, expressos succos multis ferculis variatos, ipsumque vinum suavitate vincentes, & quicquid culina, pharmacopoea, aut quaeque fere officina subministrare possit. Et hoc plerumque victu quum se ganeones infarciant, Petronius. Curavi me mox cibis validioribus, &c.ut ille ob Creseida suam, se bulbis & cochleis curavit; etiam ad Venerem se parent, & ad hanc palestram se exerceant, qui fieri possit, ut non misere depereant, Uti ille apud Schenkium, qui post potionem, uxorem & quatuor ancillas proximo cubiculo cubantes, compressit.ut non penitus insaniant? Aestuans venter cito despuit in libidinem, Hieronymus ait. Pers. Sat. 3.Post prandia, Callyroen da. Quis enim continere se potest? Siracides. Nox, & amor, vinumque nihil moderabile suadent.Luxuriosa res vinum, fomentum libidinis vocat Augustinus, blandum daemonem, Bernardus; lac veneris, Aristophanes. Non Aetna, non Vesuvius tantis ardoribus aestuant, ac juveniles medulla vino plenae, addit Epist. ad Olympiam.Hieronymus: unde ob optimum vinum Lampsacus olim Priapo sacer: & venerandi Bacchi socia, apud Hymno.Orpheum Venus audit. Haec si vinum simplex, & per se sumptum praestare possit, nam ——— Hor. lib. 3 Od. 25.quo me Bacche rapis tui plenum? Quam non insaniam, quem non furorem a caeteris expectemus? De sale lib. 1 cap. 21.Gomesius salem enumerat inter ea quae intempestivam libidinem provocare solent, Et salaciores fieri foeminas ob esum salis contendit: Venerem ideo dicunt ab Oceano ortam.

foreign.hi: Unde tot in Veneta scortorum millia cur sunt?

lg.l: In promptu causa est, est Venus orta mari.

div.p:
Et hinc foeta mater Salacea Oceani conjux, verbumque fortasse salax a sale effluxit. Mala Bacchica tantum olim in amoribus praevaluerunt, ut coronae ex illis statuae Bacchi ponerentur. Garcia ab Horto aromatum, lib. 1 cap. 28.Cubebis in vino maceratis utuntur Indi orientales ad Venerem excitandum, & Surax radix ad coitum summe facit si quis comedat, aut infusionem bibat, membrum subito erigitur. Leo Afer lib. 9 cap. ult.Surax radice Africani. Chinae radix eosdem effectus habet, talisque herbae meminit mag. nat. lib. 2 cap. 16, Quae non solum edentibus sed & genitale tangentibus tantum valet, ut coire summe desiderent, quoties fere velint, possint, alios duodecies profecisse, alios ad 60 vices pervenisse refert.Baptista Porta
ex India allatae, cujus mentionem facit & Theophrastus. Sed infinita his similia apud Rhasin, Matthiolum, Mizaldum, caeterosque medicos occurrunt, quorum ideo mentionem feci, ne quis imperitior in hos scopulos impingat, sed pro virili tanquam syrtes & cautes consulto effugiat. [In the first place, Wines prepare hearts for love.good wine, pulses, beans, roots of all types that are well prepared and sprinkled with lots of pepper, garden cardoons, lettuce, But rocket and lust-provoking onions are of no use. Nor does wanton savory help you. {Ovid}rocket, turnips, leeks, onions, pine nuts, sweet almonds, electuaries, syrups, juices, snails, shell-fish, fish excellently prepared, small birds, animal testicles, eggs, condiments of various kinds, soft beds, cushioned couches, etc. And well-nigh whatever doctors prescribe for those suffering from sexual impotence, they use it in their parties as if it were diasatyrion, and have dishes much more luxurious than these; honey-sweetened wine, choice and exotic fruit, spices, cakes, a different squeezed juice with every course, surpassing wine itself in deliciousness, and whatever the kitchen, pharmacy or almost any kind of workshop can provide. And since these gluttons commonly stuff themselves with food (I soon cured myself with stronger foodstuffs, etc. {Petronius}as he, prompted by Cressida, cured himself with onions and snails) and prepare themselves for sex and train themselves for this wrestling, how could it be otherwise than that they are miserably desperate for love, Like that man in Schenkius, who after a potion had intercourse with his wife and four maidservants sleeping in the next bedroom.and go utterly mad? ‘A raging belly soon spurts out in lust,’ says Jerome. ‘After dinner, take Callirhoe.’ Who, then, can contain himself? Night, love and wine encourage no restraint. {Ecclesiasticus}‘Wine is a wanton thing’; Augustine calls it ‘the fomenter of lust’, St Bernard ‘a seductive demon’, Aristophanes ‘the milk of love’. ‘Neither Etna nor Vesuvius burns with such flames as young men do with their marrow full of wine,’ adds Jerome: for which reason Lampsacus was once sacred to Priapus for its superlative wine, and in the Orphic hymn, Venus is named partner of the worshipful Bacchus. If unmixed wine taken on its own can be responsible for these things (‘But … where are you dragging me to, Bacchus, being full of you?’), shall we not expect madness and fury from the other things? Gomesius counts salt as one of the things which usually provoke untimely lust, ‘and contends that women are made more lustful by eating salt: for that reason, they say that Venus arose from the Ocean’.

lg.l: Why, then, are there so many thousands of whores in Venice?
The cause is clear: Venus arose from the sea.

p.ed:trans:
‘And hence came fruitful Mother Salacia, wife of Oceanus’, and perhaps the word ‘salacious’ from salt. Bacchic apples were once so influential in matters of love that they used to place crowns of them on statues of Bacchus. Cubebs macerated in wine are used in the East Indies to arouse lust, and Surax root most powerfully provokes coitus; if anyone eats it, or drinks it in an infusion, the member immediately becomes erect. {Leo Africanus}Surax root in Africa. China root has the same effects, and in Magia naturalis, Bk 2 ch. 16, Which is so effective not only for those who eat it but even for those who touch it with their genitals, so that they have an extreme desire for sex, and they can do it as often as they want; some are said to have done it twelve times, others to have managed 60 times.
Baptista Porta recalls herbs of this kind brought from India, which Theophrastus also mentions. But an infinite number of similar things appear in Rhasis, Matthiolus, Mizaldus and other physicians, which is why I have mentioned this: so that no one inexperienced should dash himself on these reefs but instead, out of caution and for the sake of his virility, he should flee from them as if they were sand-banks and savage rocks.]
